questions.q: What does an access governance model do differently from treating role-based access, least privilege, and access reviews as separate topics?
options: It connects them into one working system, where each building block reinforces the others
It replaces the need for least privilege entirely
It removes the need for any approval workflow
It applies only to privileged accounts, not ordinary roles
questions.explain: The model is explicitly the connected system: roles define access shape, least privilege constrains its size, segregation of duties constrains role combinations, and reviews verify all of it stays true over time.

questions.q: According to this lesson, where should role definitions start from?
options: Job function, with access written down and justified rather than inferred from an existing person's grant
Whoever in the department currently has the broadest access
The IT department's default new-hire template, unchanged
A list of every system in the company, granted to every role equally
questions.explain: The lesson warns against copying an existing person's access and instead calls for defining roles from the actual job function, with access justified rather than inherited.

questions.q: What is a segregation-of-duties rule, as illustrated by the vendor example?
options: A rule defining which role combinations, such as creating a vendor and approving vendor payments, must never be held by one person
A rule that requires every employee to have at least two roles
A technical setting that encrypts vendor payment data
A scheduling rule for when access reviews occur
questions.explain: Segregation of duties prevents one person from holding both halves of a sensitive process, like creating a vendor and approving payments to that vendor.

questions.q: Which two building blocks does this lesson identify as the specific gaps that allowed the Brightfield incident from the previous lesson?
options: The request and approval workflow and periodic recertification
Role definitions and least-privilege mapping
Segregation-of-duties rules and role definitions
Encryption and data masking
questions.explain: Brightfield had no approval workflow requiring a scoped justification, and no recertification cadence that would have caught the still-active login after the contract ended.

questions.q: What is 'approval fatigue,' as described in this lesson?
options: A failure mode where high-volume, low-friction approvals get rubber-stamped without genuine review
A technical limit on how many access requests a system can process per day
A benefit of frequent recertification that improves security over time
A rule preventing more than one approver from reviewing the same request
questions.explain: When approvers are overwhelmed by volume or friction, they start approving requests without genuinely checking them, which defeats the purpose of the approval step even though it exists on paper.
